newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece slams athletics boss Nebiolo on Olympic bid.
newsitem.headline: Greece slams athletics boss Nebiolo on Olympic bid.

text.p: Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos accused world athletics chief Primo Nebiolo on Tuesday of meddling in politics by disparaging Athens's bid to host the 2004 Olympics.
The Italian lawyer, who is playing a leading role in Rome's rival bid for the Games, told Greek television the Games would not solve Greece's political and economic problems.
He had already said the success of last week's world athletics championships in Athens owed more to his federation, the IAAF, than to the Greek organisers.

"Mr Nebiolo committed a gross violation of a very basic rule," the outspoken Pangalos told reporters. "Politicians are allowed to speak about sports but sports officials are not allowed to speak about politics."
"Italy uses its armed forces to deal with the terrifying problem of the mafia, which it exports to the rest of the world, like the United States and recently Albania.
"But I would never say that the mafia characterises Italy and therefore Rome does not deserve the Games. Rome will not win the Games simply because Athens is better," he added.
Greek newspapers also lashed out at Nebiolo in front-page banner headlines, calling him "Mafioso" and "Duce" -- the nickname of fascist dictator Benito Mussolini.
They accused him of shamelessly favouring Rome's bid after he told the private Mega television channel on Monday evening:
"You have many problems, economic, political...(problems) with the Maastricht treaty, the value of money and unemployment, and the Olympic Games will not solve these problems."
As the spiritual home of the Olympics, Athens was bitterly disappointed not to get the centenary Games in 1996.
Along with Rome it is now co-favourite for the 2004 Games, especially after an explosion destroyed sections of the Olympic stadium in Stockholm on Friday.
The International Olympic Committee, of which Nebiolo is a member, is due to award the Games on September 5.
Athens's bid hinged on a well-run championships. A nearly empty stadium on the first weekend was an embarrassment to organisers who blamed it on the long duration of the event and expensive tickets.
Nebiolo was quick to criticise both Greek organisers and the public. His comments prompted a flurry of reaction and he was greeted with loud boos at the closing ceremony on Sunday.

"There has maybe not been a great campaign of promotion," Nebiolo had said. "Maybe because it was on Saturday people in Athens go to the sea...They have the sea all year. They can forget the sea for a week."
Seats were promptly filled and observers praised the event's efficiency. But Nebiolo told Mega this was mainly due to the IAAF, and that the Greek organisers were "mediocre".
Athens Mayor Dimitris Avramopoulos and Greek Olympic Committee head Lambis Nicolaou accused Nebiolo of painting Greece as a troubled nation to promote Rome's Olympic candidacy.
The other candidates for the 2004 Games are Cape Town and Buenos Aires.
